competitors.name: iLovePDF
competitors.model: Freemium, free tier capped, Premium $5/mo billed annually ($60/yr) or $9/mo monthly; Business custom for 25+ users
competitors.note: Best-known consumer brand alongside Smallpdf; clean and fast when it works. Free tier caps merge/split/compress at 100MB per task, merge at 25 files, image-to-PDF at 40MB, PDF-to-JPG at 25MB, and most tools at 1 to 2 tasks. Everything is uploaded. Free users get ads and the upload wait; reviewers cite 'slow speeds and limits' and 'ads and clunky UIs waste time' (mirrorreview.com).

competitors.name: Smallpdf
competitors.model: Freemium, free capped (widely reported as ~2 tasks/day, some tools 2/hour), Pro variously listed at $9-$15/mo, Team ~$7 to 12/user/mo
competitors.note: The polish leader; Swiss-based, best-in-category UI, which is why people pay. Free tier is the sore spot ('the free version limits how much you can do in a day… you'll hit that wall pretty fast', SoftwareAdvice). Serious billing-trust damage: 2.2/5 on SmartCustomer (6 reviews), 1.0/5 on ComplaintsBoard (5 complaints, 0% resolved), with repeated unauthorized-charge and no-refund reports. Also 'compress on free barely compresses at all… strong compression preset is premium only' (AlternativeTo).

competitors.name: Adobe Acrobat online (free tools)
competitors.model: 'Free' tools gated by sign-in and transaction limits; Acrobat Standard/Pro subscription roughly $13-$25/mo or $180-$300/yr (HowToGeek, MakeUseOf)
competitors.note: Owns the trust halo, people search 'Adobe' when they don't know what else to use, and owns the color red. But it is the archetype of the last-step paywall: Adobe's own community has a thread titled 'Why not free when it says free?' noting the free merge tool caps at 1,500 combined pages, and another explaining 'you have used your one free transaction for the current 7-day period.' Sign-in required to get your file back.

competitors.name: PDF24 Tools
competitors.model: Genuinely free and unlimited, ad-supported; free PDF24 Creator desktop app for offline use
competitors.note: The most honest incumbent and the one that actually undercuts a paid tier: 25+ tools, 'free of charge and without any restrictions,' no watermark, no account required (SmashingApps names it the best free no-watermark editor). Weaknesses: online tools still upload to PDF24 servers ('file transfers are encrypted… files completely removed after a short time'), it monetizes with on-page advertising, and its UI is repeatedly called dated, 'UI feels outdated compared to Smallpdf.' Beating PDF24 is a design problem, not a pricing problem.

competitors.name: Sejda
competitors.model: Free tier hard-capped; paid web plans; Sejda Desktop for local processing
competitors.note: Publishes its limits honestly on every tool page: 'Free service for documents up to 50 pages or 50 MB and 3 tasks per hour.' Also markets the exact promise we're making, 'Rather not upload your files and work with them offline? Try Sejda Desktop… the files never leave your computer', but charges for it and requires an install. We give that away in a browser tab.

competitors.name: Stirling PDF
competitors.model: Open source / open-core, free to self-host; Docker, desktop, or private server
competitors.note: 89.2k GitHub stars, 50+ tools, 40+ languages, the enthusiast's answer. Dominates the privacy conversation on HN (507 pts / 231 comments in 2023; 366 pts in 2024) and is called 'open source gold standard for any pdf needs.' Irrelevant to our actual user: it needs Docker or a NAS. Nobody with a portal deadline in 10 minutes is spinning up a container.

competitors.name: macOS Preview / iOS Files, the 'good enough' free competitor
competitors.note: This is the real competitor, not the funded startup. On a Mac, Preview already does merge, drag-thumbnail reorder, rotate and delete natively and well, which is why Mac users never search for this. Windows is where the market is: the Microsoft Tech Community thread 'how to merge pdf files into one on Windows without Adobe Acrobat' concludes 'Windows doesn't have a built-in feature for merging PDFs,' with answers pointing to PDFgear, PDFsam, PDFtk, Ghostscript, a Word Insert>Object trick, and Print-to-PDF ('not recommended for frequent or complex merging'). Our audience is Windows, ChromeOS, and phone users, and people on locked-down work/library machines.

competitors.name: The client-side clone swarm (pdfly.uk, offlinepdf.com, pdf.makr.io, kittokit, OneClickPDF, Drawboard, pdfux, plus smallpdf.us / smallpdf.co.uk / smallpdf.online lookalikes)
competitors.model: Free, no account, monetization usually unstated (SEO/ads/upsell)
competitors.note: Our actual competitive set, and the reason positioning is hard: 'no upload, no signup, no watermark' is now boilerplate marketing copy, asserted by dozens of near-identical sites including S3-hosted pages squatting on the Smallpdf name. Some are real and good, offlinepdf.com renders true thumbnails via pdf.js with pdf-lib and states 'zero bytes leave your device'; pdfly.uk lists 56 tools with 'no file size limits.' The claim is free to make, so it no longer differentiates. Proof does.

complaints.complaint: The last-step ambush: you do all the work, then the download is gated. Adobe's own support forum has a thread literally titled 'Why not free when it says free?', and another Adobe answer explains 'if you sign in on a Monday for the first time and use the Convert PDF to Word tool, you have used your one free transaction for the current 7-day period.' Competitors now market directly against this, Drawboard's tagline is 'no uploads, no sign-ups, no surprises at the last step.'
complaints.source: community.adobe.com threads (surfaced via SERP snippets); drawboard.com/tools/merge-pdfs marketing copy
complaints.weWinIf: Zero interstitial between 'done' and the file landing in Downloads. No modal, no email capture, no 'rate us', no tip prompt on the download path. Show the output filename and byte size next to the button BEFORE they press it, so there is visibly nothing left to happen. The tip jar lives in the footer and never on the critical path.

complaints.complaint: Daily/hourly task counters that stop you mid-job. 'You can only compress 2 PDFs in an hour unless you pay $6 per month.' 'The free version also limits how much you can do in a day, so if you're working with a bunch of files, you'll hit that wall pretty fast.' Sejda states it in the product: 'Free service for documents up to 50 pages or 50 MB and 3 tasks per hour.'
complaints.source: smartcustomer.com/reviews/smallpdf.com (May 2018 review); softwareadvice.com Smallpdf reviews; sejda.com tool pages; candyfile.io/blog/smallpdf-alternatives ('most tools cap free users at 2 tasks per day')
complaints.weWinIf: Say the quiet part loudly where competitors put their pricing table: there is no counter because there is no server to meter you. A person who just got told 'you've reached your free limit' elsewhere should be able to confirm in three seconds that it can't happen here.

complaints.complaint: Free-trial billing traps and refusal to refund. 'I signed up for a free trial and was charged unintentionally… they referred to the terms and conditions and said I'm stuck with the year and they will not provide a refund' (Dec 2024). 'They will hiddenly charge you without any notification until you catch them!' (Feb 2024). ComplaintsBoard has users reporting $108, $144 and £81 taken without authorization, 0 of 5 complaints resolved.
complaints.weWinIf: There is no payment surface at all, no card field, no trial, no 'upgrade' button anywhere in the UI. Make the tip link visually a link, not a CTA button, and word it so it's obviously post-hoc gratitude, not a gate. This is the cheapest trust win available and costs us nothing.

complaints.complaint: People are actively scared of uploading these specific documents. On HN: 'I've been looking for something like this to self-host, to avoid my partner uploading sensitive documents to random PDF manipulation websites.' The FBI Denver Field Office issued a public warning on 7 March 2025 that free online document-converter tools are being used to deliver malware, leading to ransomware and identity theft, covered by Malwarebytes, CSO Online, 9News and Boulder Daily Camera.
complaints.source: news.ycombinator.com item 38765627 (Stirling-PDF, 507 pts / 231 comments); fbi.gov Denver field office advisory 2025-03-07 as reported by malwarebytes.com, csoonline.com (article 3853045), 9news.com, dailycamera.com
complaints.weWinIf: Don't just claim no-upload, make it falsifiable in the UI. A short, plain line the user can act on: 'Turn off your Wi-Fi. It still works.' Ship as an installable PWA that genuinely runs offline, keep the CSP with no external origins, and link the source. Post-FBI-advisory, verifiability is the product.

complaints.complaint: 'No upload / no signup / no watermark' has become meaningless boilerplate. The first page of results for merge queries is wall-to-wall near-identical sites making the identical claim, including clones squatting on incumbent names, smallpdf.us ('No account, no paywall'), smallpdf.co.uk ('100% serverless client-side architecture'), and a Smallpdf-branded page hosted on a raw S3 bucket. A user cannot tell us apart from a malware site by reading our marketing copy.
complaints.source: Bing and DuckDuckGo SERPs for 'smallpdf free limit' and 'merge pdf no upload' (smallpdf.us, smallpdf.co.uk, smallpdf.online, smallpdf-rfree.s3.amazonaws.com)
complaints.weWinIf: Trade slogans for evidence: a named studio with a real About page, a visible privacy page, an offline-verification prompt, a link to the source, and a 'what this page loaded' list showing every request came from one origin. Looking generic is now a liability, not neutral.

complaints.complaint: Upload waits, size ceilings, and ads eat the time you were trying to save. iLovePDF caps merge at 25 files / 100MB and publishes its own troubleshooting article for 'file too large to upload'; reviewers report 'slow speeds and limits' and that 'ads and clunky UIs waste time.' A whole competitor landing page exists titled 'Frustrated with iLovePDF's popups, ads, and file uploads?'
complaints.weWinIf: Time-to-first-thumbnail is the entire pitch. Files should be visible as pages within a second of drop, because there is no round trip. No ad slot, no cookie banner, no consent modal, those are the visual signature of the sites people are fleeing.

complaints.complaint: Drag-to-reorder is broken or missing in the tools that supposedly have it. Adobe UserVoice: 'BUG Drag and Drop Not Working in PAGE THUMBNAILS. Drag and Drop has stopped working in Page thumbnail. Cannot rearrange pages in page thumbnail.' Adobe Community: 'Acrobat will not allow me to drag and drop pages from one open pdf to another' after a subscription upgrade; 'I can no longer drag pages from the Pages Thumbnail sidebar onto my desktop.'
complaints.weWinIf: Drag must work, and must never be the only way. Every reorder available via drag is also available via keyboard (grab/move/drop with arrow keys), explicit buttons, 'move to top/bottom', and a type-a-number 'move to position' for documents too long to drag through.

complaints.complaint: On phones, reordering degrades to a worse experience and competitors admit it. kittokit's own instructions: 'On mobile, tap to select then use the Top/Bottom or up/down buttons.' Meanwhile a real chunk of demand is explicitly mobile, 'Reorder PDF Pages on iPhone & iPad, Free, No App Needed' is a live search target.
complaints.weWinIf: Treat touch as the primary case, not the fallback: long-press to lift with edge autoscroll, plus tap-to-select-then-tap-destination (which beats dragging for a 40-page doc anyway), 44px+ targets, and no hover-only affordances. Thumbnails must stay big enough to identify a page on a 390px screen.

complaints.complaint: Browser-based tools die on real-world file sizes, which is the standing objection to our entire architecture. 'Three 80 MB PDFs = 240 MB sitting in RAM… Browser tab crashes.' Microsoft Q&A: 'High CPU usage and short freezes when processing large PDFs in a browser are expected to a degree, because the work is done by JavaScript/WebAssembly in the tab.' pdf.js issue #14679 documents OOM at 130MB / 25k pages. Even Smallpdf's web app has this: 'whenever I try to OCR very large files or very many files, it crashes because a web browser just can't handle that much processing.'
complaints.source: dev.to/sunshey 'How to Merge Large PDFs in the Browser Without Crashing'; learn.microsoft.com Q&A 5843813; github.com/mozilla/pdf.js issue 14679; capterra.com Smallpdf reviews
complaints.weWinIf: Never load everything at once. Lazy-render thumbnails in a viewport window, do the work in a Web Worker so the UI never locks, show real progress with a working cancel, and warn honestly at the point of drop ('this is 180 MB, thumbnails will take a moment') instead of presenting a frozen tab. A graceful slow path beats a dead one.

complaints.complaint: Tools silently fail on files the user considers normal, encrypted, password-protected, or malformed PDFs. 'It can only open half of my PDFs so it is a terrible product' (Dec 2024). Bank statements, payslips and government forms are frequently password-protected, and these are exactly the files being merged for portals.
complaints.weWinIf: Name the failure and give a route out: 'This PDF is password-protected. Enter the open password, or open it in your PDF reader and re-save without protection.' Our repo README already promises 'password-protected PDFs get an honest explanation instead of a crash', keep that, and make the message actionable rather than merely honest.

complaints.complaint: The free unlimited option that already exists looks like 2011, so people pay for polish they shouldn't have to. PDF24 is free, unlimited, watermark-free and account-free, yet is repeatedly dismissed with 'UI feels outdated compared to Smallpdf.'
complaints.weWinIf: Be the first tool that is simultaneously the most generous AND the best-looking. Our differentiation is not 'free', PDF24 is already free. It's 'free, nothing uploaded, and it feels better than the $15/month one.' Design quality is the moat here, not the terms.

tableStakes: Rendered page thumbnails, actual visual previews of each page, not text labels. VERIFIED GAP IN OUR BUILD: /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps/pdf-tools/app.js renders each page as a list row reading 'Page 3' plus a filename with ↑/↓/⟳/× buttons, and the app ships only vendor-pdf-lib.js with no pdf.js. Every credible competitor (offlinepdf.com, Sejda, Adobe, Smallpdf, Preview) shows a thumbnail grid. Users are visually verifying 'is that the signed page?', a text list cannot answer that, and its absence is the single thing that will read as amateur.

Drag-to-reorder those thumbnails, with a keyboard path and explicit buttons as equal-status alternatives (not fallbacks), including 'move to top', 'move to bottom', and 'move to position N' for documents too long to drag through.

Cross-file page-level assembly: pages from several files visible together in one output-order grid, each chip labelled with its source filename, so a user can interleave rather than merge-then-reorder in two separate steps.
Rotate one page, rotate a selection, and rotate all, with rotation shown on the thumbnail itself, and stacking correctly past 360°.

Multi-select: shift-click a range, ctrl/cmd-click individual pages, select-all, and a typed range syntax ('3-8, 12, 20-') for bulk delete, rotate, or extract. Doing 40 pages one click at a time is the classic amateur tell.
Undo, at minimum for page deletion, ideally a full undo/redo stack. Deleting the wrong page of a mortgage packet with no way back is the worst thing this app can do to someone.

Split with named, previewed modes: every page into its own file, split at page N, split into custom ranges, extract just the selection, plus a plain-language preview of exactly which files will come out and what they'll be called.
Control over the output filename and a visible output size before download, with a download that preserves that name. Users are usually feeding a portal with naming and size rules.
Progress with a real cancel for large files, and honest, specific handling of password-protected and malformed PDFs instead of a spinner or a crash.
Works fully offline as an installable PWA, on a phone, with 44px+ targets, no hover-only controls, no account, no watermark on output, and no ads or cookie banner.
differentiators: Make the privacy claim falsifiable instead of asserted. A quiet, permanent line the user can act on in five seconds, 'Turn your Wi-Fi off. It still works.', plus an offline-ready PWA and an optional 'what this page loaded' panel listing every request and its origin. Every competitor makes the claim; only a static single-origin app can invite the test. Post-FBI-advisory this is the highest-value thing we own.

Publish an explicit negative-space list exactly where competitors put a pricing table: no account, no upload, no daily limit, no file-size cap, no watermark, no ads, no card on file, no surprise at the last step. Each line answers a documented, sourced complaint. It costs us nothing and is structurally uncopyable by anyone paying for servers.

Thumbnails that are actually legible, noticeably larger than the 60 to 80px chips the category uses, with tap/hover to peek at a full-size page. The job is visual verification of specific pages under time pressure, and every competitor under-sizes this.

'Fit the portal' output sizing tied to the real caps people hit: a live readout ('your file is 14.2 MB, 2.2 MB over') with presets for the actual thresholds (USCIS 12 MB, common 5/10 MB portals) and a compress-to-target path. IRCC's own help page states the underlying constraint plainly: 'You can only upload 1 file per field.' Nobody frames the tool around the deadline that caused the visit.

One canvas, not a tool grid. Competitors present 25 to 56 separate tools and make you pick before you've seen your document; our core.js already models the right thing (a docs array plus a flat output order with per-page rotation), so drop files first, then merge/reorder/rotate/delete/split are all just operations on one visible order. That is a genuinely different mental model and it's already half-built.

Remember the last recipe in localStorage with no account, 'last time you split every 1 page' or 'you usually name output merged.pdf'. Repeat users are doing the same bureaucratic task monthly, and personalization without a login is precisely the thing account-based competitors can't beat us on.

Honest failure as a feature. Encrypted PDF, broken xref, 400 MB monster: name the cause, name the fix, offer the next step. Since 'it can only open half of my PDFs' is a real 1-star review of the market leader, a visibly better failure surface is a cheap and memorable win.

Ship it as the best-looking tool in the category, not just the most generous one. PDF24 already owns free-and-unlimited and is dismissed for looking dated; beating it is a design job, and our only real competitive risk is looking like the clone swarm we're standing next to in search results.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: The category is red. Adobe Acrobat is #F40F02, iLovePDF is red, Smallpdf is crimson, red plus a white card on light grey is the visual default, and using it now reads as knockoff rather than credible, especially since the SERP is full of literal Smallpdf-branded clones on S3 buckets. The standard layout is a marketing landing page first (hero, illustration, 'trusted by N million', cookie banner, ad rail) followed by a grid of 25 to 56 rainbow-gradient tool tiles, an oversized dashed dropzone, and, once you're in, page chips too small to identify anything. Dated tells: the rainbow tool grid, skeuomorphic drop-shadowed document illustrations, gradient buttons, stock imagery of smiling people with laptops, a narrow centered column that wastes desktop width while the thumbnails stay tiny, and any interstitial between finishing and downloading. What reads as current in 2026: content-first pages that show the working surface immediately with no landing preamble, near-flat high-contrast neutral surfaces, exactly one accent used for state rather than decoration, generous whitespace, system/variable type at comfortable sizes, calm and transparent interfaces, accessibility-first defaults, and real dark-mode support rather than an inverted afterthought. Because the field is flooded with near-identical low-trust clones, generic now actively signals danger, visual specificity is a trust signal, not a vanity one.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: Nobody opens a PDF tool for fun. The trigger is almost always an external deadline colliding with a rejecting upload box: a portal that accepts one file per field (Canada's IRCC states exactly that), a USCIS 12 MB cap, a job application wanting resume and cover letter as one document, a mortgage packet, a court filing, an insurance claim, a Canvas assignment. The user is mid-task and mildly panicked, often at 11pm before a midnight cutoff, frequently on a work, school, or library machine where they cannot install software, which is the entire reason they are in a browser at all rather than using a desktop app. The documents are usually private: tax returns, payslips, medical records, passport scans, divorce paperwork. Many users are non-technical and over 40, or are the family's designated computer person doing this on a parent's behalf. Practically, this dictates: the drop zone visible in the first screen with no scrolling and no landing copy; thumbnails large enough to identify a page at a glance without zooming, because the actual cognitive task is 'is that the signed one?'; body text at 16 to 17px minimum and page labels that stay legible on a bad office monitor and on a phone in daylight; 44px+ targets with no hover-only controls; destructive actions that are recoverable; contrast well above the minimum rather than fashionably low; and no entrance animations, skeleton shimmer, or celebratory confetti, every millisecond of delight is friction to someone with eight minutes left. The register is clerical competence, not cheer. It should feel like a well-run records office: calm, exact, unhurried, and completely uninterested in your attention.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: quiet, clerical, precise, unhurried, trustworthy, matter-of-fact

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Deep indigo-navy ink (a near-black blue-violet, low chroma, dark value) as the brand and interactive color, on a warm bone/parchment ground rather than a cool one, with a single antique-brass note reserved exclusively for selection/active-page state. Think fountain-pen ink on manila, not SaaS blue on white.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Three forces decide this. (1) Category: red is owned outright by Adobe (#F40F02), iLovePDF and Smallpdf, and in a search results page full of Smallpdf clones, red now reads as counterfeit, the one hue we must not touch. (2) Portfolio: I audited all 23 apps in /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps. The cool-pastel band is saturated, team-parent #2a67bd/#95c0ff, pill-schedule #78c9f5, bill-splitter #78cce3, packing-list #60d4ca, scan-to-pdf #5dd2db, baby-log #6c5d9d, seating-chart #7d549a, image-compressor #8e479a, and greens (grocery-list, home-inventory, qr-maker, sub-plans) and warm oranges (signup-sheets #ffa65f, specials-planner #fda387, moving-boxes #e3b47a) are equally full. At 23 apps, pure hue uniqueness is gone, so differentiate on hue AND value AND temperature together: a near-black indigo at low chroma sits nowhere near team-parent's mid-blue or baby-log's pale lavender by value alone, and pairing it with a warm ground is the decisive separator, since every cool-accent app in the portfolio also uses a cool canvas. (3) Function, which is the strongest argument: the most important objects in this UI are page thumbnails, and page thumbnails are white rectangles. The current build sits on --canvas:#f5f7ff with --accent:#6d78d1, a cool blue-white ground that makes white paper float ambiguously against it. A warm bone ground (the portfolio's existing #fef6ea family, pulled slightly cooler and greyer, roughly #f4f0e8) gives every page somewhere to sit, so the thumbnail grid gains structure for free. It also reads as paper, file cabinet, records office, exactly the clerical calm the emotional context calls for. Practically: keep the existing token structure in index.html, deepen --accent from #6d78d1 toward a #2f3563-to-#3a4270 range, swap --canvas/--canvas-2 from cool to warm neutral, keep surfaces near-white so thumbnails read as paper-on-desk, and reserve a single brass tone (~#b08339) for selected pages only, never for buttons, never decoratively. One accent for identity, one for state, nothing else.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Red, crimson and orange-red in any brand role, Adobe, iLovePDF and Smallpdf own it, and post-FBI-advisory a red-branded knockoff PDF site is exactly the silhouette users have been warned about. Generic SaaS mid-blue (#2563EB and neighbours), it is the default everyone reaches for, and team-parent already holds that slot in this portfolio. The current cool blue-white canvas #f5f7ff, it is the single most consequential mistake in the existing build, because it robs white page thumbnails of contrast against their own background. Pastel lavender and violet, baby-log, seating-chart and image-compressor already occupy that band. Bronze or tan as the primary hue, moving-boxes (#e3b47a/#8e5d11) and signup-sheets (#ffa65f/#9c5300) are too close; brass works only as a small state accent. Rainbow-coded tool tiles, the defining dated tell of the category. Pure #000 on #fff across large surfaces, harsh for the sustained thumbnail-scanning this app demands, often under office fluorescents. Low-contrast grey-on-grey 'minimal' styling, this user is stressed and possibly on a poor monitor; contrast is a functional requirement, not a taste choice. And never let colour alone distinguish a destructive page action from a safe one: delete needs an icon, a label and an undo, not just a red tint, since the cost of an accidental deletion here is someone's mortgage packet.

confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH overall, with specific gaps the designer should know about. METHOD CAVEAT: the WebSearch tool reported its per-session budget already exhausted (200/200) before I made a single call, so no native searches were possible. All research was done via WebFetch against DuckDuckGo Lite and Bing RSS result pages plus direct page fetches, roughly 30 fetches. That worked, but it changes what I could see. BIGGEST GAP, REDDIT: this environment blocks www.reddit.com, old.reddit.com and www.redditmedia.com outright, and a redlib mirror returned 403. I could read Reddit thread titles and SERP snippets but never read a thread. So Reddit sentiment here is second-hand; if you want the richest gripe texture, someone should open r/pdf and r/Acrobat manually. HIGH CONFIDENCE (multiple independent sources or primary pages): the FBI Denver advisory of 7 March 2025 on malware-bearing free file-converter sites (fbi.gov itself 403'd me, but Malwarebytes, CSO Online, 9News and Boulder Daily Camera all report it independently); Sejda's published free limits (50 pages / 50 MB / 3 tasks per hour, stated on Sejda's own tool pages); iLovePDF's free caps and $5-billed-annually / $9-monthly pricing (ilovepdf.com/pricing directly); PDF24 being free, unlimited, ad-supported and server-side with an offline desktop alternative (tools.pdf24.org directly); Stirling PDF's 89.2k stars and positioning (GitHub directly); Windows having no built-in merge (Microsoft Tech Community thread); IRCC's 'You can only upload 1 file per field' (ircc.canada.ca directly); the Adobe drag-and-drop thumbnail bugs (Adobe UserVoice and Adobe Community titles). HIGHEST CONFIDENCE OF ALL: the thumbnail gap in our own app, I read /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps/pdf-tools/app.js and index.html directly. It renders a text list ('Page 3' + filename + ↑/↓/⟳/×), ships only vendor-pdf-lib.js with no pdf.js, and uses --accent:#6d78d1 on --canvas:#f5f7ff. That is verified fact, not inference. The 23-app palette audit is likewise from the repo, though I sampled top hex frequencies per index.html rather than reading each design system, so treat those as indicative accents. MEDIUM CONFIDENCE: Smallpdf's exact free cap and price. Sources contradict each other, '2 tasks per day' (candyfile), '2 per hour' (SmartCustomer, 2018), and $9 / $12 / $15 per month across toolradar, getpulsesignal and aiproductivity. smallpdf.com/pricing itself truncated on fetch. Treat as 'capped, roughly $9 to 15/mo', not gospel. Adobe's free-tier limits ('one free transaction for the current 7-day period', 1,500-page merge cap) come from Adobe Support Community posts via SERP snippets, not Adobe's current fine print, adobe.com/acrobat/online/merge-pdf.html timed out twice. Adobe subscription pricing ($13 to 25/mo, $180 to 300/yr) is from HowToGeek and MakeUseOf, not Adobe. LOW CONFIDENCE / FLAGGED AS SELF-SERVING: practicalwebtools.com's audit ('8 of 12 converters retain files 24h+', '4 of 12 may access contents for service improvement') is a competing tool's own marketing blog, directionally consistent with the FBI advisory but not independent, so do not quote its numbers publicly. Same for candyfile.io's comparison table. NOT VERIFIED AT ALL: Trustpilot (403) and G2 (inaccessible), Smallpdf sentiment rests on ComplaintsBoard (n=5, 1.0/5) and SmartCustomer (n=6, 2.2/5), which are tiny, self-selecting, complaint-seeking samples. The billing-trap complaints are real and quotable but should not be characterised as representative of typical Smallpdf users. I also could not read Play Store or App Store 1 to 3 star reviews directly (JS-rendered, unfetchable), so mobile-app-specific gripes are inferred from web sources rather than observed, and the mobile drag-and-drop finding rests mainly on how competitors describe their own mobile fallbacks."
